t: Researcher positionality statements in applied linguistics
abs: This study investigates how reflexive positionality is enacted in researcher positionality statements (RPSs) across twenty-two applied linguistics (AL) and language education journals (all SSCI Q1), focusing on how researchers articulate their positionality in relation to other dimensions of reflexivity, including disciplinary knowledge, relationships with research participants, methodological choices, and textual representation. Guided by methodological scholarship on self-reflexivity, we analyze 387 empirical articles to examine how reflexivity is rhetorically constructed and interrelated in RPSs, describing overall trends and patterns of reflexive positioning. Based on these patterns, we present our findings as a continuum of reflexive enactment, illustrating variation in the depth, relationality, and dynamism with which positionality is taken up in published research. We discuss that approaching researcher positionality through the lens of enactment shifts attention away from whether reflexivity is present and toward how reflexive work is made visible within AL research. Therefore, RPSs are not simply sites of disclosure, but rhetorical and relational spaces in which scholars negotiate disciplinary norms, ethical commitments, and understandings of knowledge production.

t: Conversation by design: repair and interactional competence in L2 talk with an AI speaking application
abs: AI-powered speaking applications invite second language learners into extended spoken exchanges marketed as conversational practice. Drawing on conversation analysis, this study asks what kind of interactional environment such applications provide for learners bringing human interactional competence to a machine partner. Analysis of eighty-four screen-recorded sessions between six Korean EFL learners and the application Speak documents three patterns. Where a learner’s response displays a misunderstanding of the prior question, no third-position repair occurs; the response is ratified and built upon. Where automatic speech recognition registers a turn as different words than the learner produced, learners repair with variable success or let the divergence pass. In an extended case, repeated repair fails, and the learner states explicitly that shared understanding cannot be reached. The application’s turn design allocates no sequential position for repair-relevant work, displacing that labor onto the learner. We argue that what these applications afford is therefore closer to monologic production than to conversational practice, and claims made for such tools in language curricula should be calibrated accordingly.

t: Task repetition and orientation in L2 oral narratives: a communication/content/function-focused analysis
abs: This study examined how task repetition (performing the same task across multiple occasions) and task orientation (directed attention to linguistic form vs. message content) shape L2 learners’ oral narrative performance. Learners’ output was evaluated using the communication, content, and function (CCF) framework, which captures how speakers structure information, express meanings, and organize discourse. Chinese undergraduate learners were randomly assigned to a grammar-focused group (n = 35), a content-focused group (n = 34), and an audience-directed group (n = 35). Participants retold the same episodic narrative three times over 3 weeks, with varying task orientations. Results show that task repetition significantly enhanced learners’ ability to structure messages, express evaluative stance, and organize temporal and logical sequences, with small to medium effect sizes. In contrast, task orientation had limited impact on overall performance, though the grammar-focused group showed selective gains in direct speech and more appropriate referential choices. These findings demonstrate that repeated task performance strengthens learners’ construction and organization of meaning, supporting the pedagogical value of incorporating functionally oriented analysis of learner output into L2 speaking instruction.

t: Examining the role of interindividual and intraindividual variability in syntactic complexity development across repeated independent and integrated writing tasks
abs: This study examined the effects of task repetition on L2 writing in independent and integrated tasks at inter- and intraindividual levels, focusing on syntactic complexity as a multidimensional construct. Forty-one undergraduates completed repeated writing tasks over nine weeks, and their essays were analyzed using fine-grained clausal and phrasal indices. Linear mixed-effects models assessed inter- and intraindividual variability over time, capturing both between-learner differences and within-learner change. For the intraindividual analyses, person-specific growth slopes and residual-based variability estimates were used to examine variability–development associations. Results showed substantial interindividual variability in syntactic complexity across both tasks, along with meaningful intraindividual variability across performances. Task type exerted a strong effect: integrated tasks elicited lower clausal complexity but denser noun phrase elaboration than independent tasks. Longitudinal development was domain-specific: clausal complexity remained largely stable, whereas selected phrasal indices, particularly adjectival and noun–noun modification, showed clearer positive change. Task-related modulation of developmental patterns was limited, with only isolated phrasal constructions showing task-specific patterns. After correction for multiple comparisons, no reliable variability–growth association was found for the clausal indices, whereas task-dependent associations emerged for adjectival and determiner modification in the phrasal domain.

t: Tackling linguistic discrimination in higher education: a student-staff collaborative approach
abs: The field has long been committed to critically exploring the role of language in systemic inequality and social injustice. More recently, a growing body of research has explored these issues not just as ‘real-world’ problems but also as issues in Higher Education (HE). This article adds to this work by introducing a staff–student collaborative model which is designed to tackle linguistic discrimination in HE. The approach, which we have implemented at the University of Edinburgh, engages student societies that campaign for the rights of working-class and state-educated students as language activists. We provide an overview of our strategy focussing on three main activities: (1) student-led campaigns that combine lived experiences with academic research, (2) two large-scale events that bring together researchers, students, and stakeholders, and (3) continuing professional development courses that provide explicit training in identifying and tackling linguistic discrimination in the classroom. Through this discussion, we demonstrate that a collaborative enterprise between staff and students committed to addressing structural and social inequality can be a transformational force in addressing linguistic discrimination in HE.

t: Digital linguistic imperialism: can we decolonize English when the AI writing tools are colonial?
abs: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into language learning presents a paradox: while promising democratization, they often reinforce linguistic hegemony. Through a methodological innovation, this study employed a 12-week critical post-human ethnography in an Iranian English as a Foreign Language (EFL) context, combining algorithmic audits of Grammarly, QuillBot, and ChatGPT with classroom observations of 23 MA EFL advanced university students (including screen recordings, interviews, and think-aloud protocols) and a counter-infrastructure co-design workshop. Drawing primarily on frameworks of infrastructural violence and agential realism, with data colonialism and a contextualized understanding of raciolinguistic ideology serving as contextual lenses, results indicate AI tools function as colonial infrastructures that systematically pathologize non-Inner Circle linguistic features, eliciting responses ranging from linguistic shame to defiance. Crucially, co-designing a localized micro-model validated translingual identities and enabled infrastructural sovereignty. The study contributes a novel methodological framework for auditing digital linguistic imperialism and proposes a decolonial post-human pedagogy centered on infrastructural co-governance.

t: Social representations of English materialized in the use of anglicisms in Brazilian Portuguese
abs: This article investigates the social representations of English materialized in the use of anglicisms in Brazilian Portuguese, drawing on research with fifty-five teacher education students enrolled in a Portuguese–English programme at Universidade Federal Fluminense, a public federal university in south-eastern Brazil. While previous studies have examined anglicisms primarily as lexical borrowings or indicators of globalization, less attention has been paid to their role as discursive practices through which social representations are constructed and negotiated. A mixed-methods design combined a structured questionnaire and semistructured interviews, analysed through the lenses of sociolinguistics, glottopolitics, and translanguaging. The results suggested that English representations did not differ substantially between beginners and seniors, indicating that they were largely shaped outside formal academic contexts. The findings point to three interrelated axes of representation—access to knowledge, social and professional advancement, and the construction of cultural identities—which emerge from participants’ reported practices. Simultaneously, the data highlight the tensions between English as a resource and a potential mechanism of exclusion, reflecting broader inequalities in access to language learning.

t: From theory to practice: the impact of ELF communication strategy instruction in an EMI context
abs: Communication strategies (CS) that enhance mutual understanding and relationship management are crucial to successful ELF communication. Although prior research recommends including CS in ELF-informed pedagogy, few empirical studies have investigated the effects of such instruction, resulting in a lack of evidence-based guidance for practitioners who wish to include ELF CS to meet their learners’ real-world communicative needs. This study developed and investigated the effectiveness of instructional materials and assessment instruments for teaching six communication strategies that have been reported in ELF descriptive literature. A sequential, quasi-experimental, mixed-methods design was implemented at a university in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, where ELF is used for academic purposes (ELFA). Participants’ receptive and productive skills were assessed, and self-reported transfer of learning to authentic communication as well as potential reasons for learning outcomes were also explored. The results suggest that ELF CS are viable pedagogical targets in global ELFA contexts. The findings provide guidance for instructors and curriculum developers who aim to provide ELF-informed instruction, as well as highlighting important directions for future research in this area.

t: Investigating EFL learners’ knowledge of the grammatical functions of high-frequency verbs
abs: This study investigated Japanese English as a Foreign Language learners’ knowledge of the grammatical functions of vocabulary, focusing on high-frequency verbs from the first three 1,000-word frequency levels. A total of 212 Japanese university students completed a grammaticality judgment task consisting of 42 high-frequency verbs used both correctly and incorrectly with respect to their grammatical functions. Participants rated each sentence on a six-point scale. The results indicated that learners’ overall knowledge of verbs’ grammatical functions was limited, with learners’ judgment ratings aligning with item grammaticality in only 58.9 per cent of cases. Importantly, no significant differences in grammaticality ratings were observed across verb frequency levels, suggesting that learners lacked reliable knowledge of grammatical functions even for verbs in the first 1,000-word frequency band. In contrast, proficiency played a significant role, with higher-proficiency learners demonstrating more appropriate sensitivity to grammaticality, particularly for more frequent verbs. These findings suggest that the grammatical functions of verbs may be less strongly influenced by word frequency than other dimensions of vocabulary knowledge. The study highlights the need for explicit instruction targeting the grammatical aspects of vocabulary knowledge.

t: Lexico-syntactic complexity and accuracy in heritage language learners at different proficiency levels: a cross-sectional study
abs: Research on second language (L2) learning using complexity measures has identified key developmental parameters with practical implications for language instruction and related fields. These parameters, however, might not necessarily apply to heritage language learners whose linguistic profile is different from that of L2 learners. This study addresses that gap by analyzing several complexity measures in Spanish heritage language samples. These measures include accuracy, and lexical and syntactic complexity in written texts produced by Spanish heritage language learners enrolled in college-level heritage language courses in the United States. The samples represent writers at four different ACTFL-based functional proficiency levels: Intermediate Mid, Intermediate High, Advanced Low, and Advanced Mid. The results showed a linear increment in accuracy as proficiency increases. Additionally, the study found changes in lexical and syntactic domains at the transition between Intermediate sublevels, whereas Advanced learners demonstrated greater sensitivity to changes in lexical measures. Taken together, the findings indicate that accuracy and text length are the strongest correlates of ACTFL-based functional proficiency sub-level in this group of HLLs.

t: Imagining and anticipating institutional linguistic justice in schools
abs: Linguistic justice as a named concept in applied linguistics and related fields receives a growing amount of scholarly attention, especially concerning educational contexts. Yet use of the term often relies on theories of change which frame pedagogical interventions and diversity training as a solution for achieving linguistic justice, typically overlooking the need for structural and institutional transformation. Here, I draw on the speculative methodology of imagination infrastructure to propose a set of design principles for the creation of linguistically just schools at an institutional level. Rooted in place-based activism, this prefigurative and anticipatory vision for institutional linguistic justice incorporates the nonlinguistic factors that lie at the root of structural discrimination, embodies cross-movement solidarity to situate linguistic justice in partnership with other social justice struggles, dismantles linguistic hierarchies and associated relations of power, and accompanies schools in the design of new worlds. Ultimately, this vision pushes for the creation of capacities and conditions that bring different and desired futures into the present.

t: ‘Identify, Undo, Heal, Resist, Fight’: a continuum of organizational discourse moves in countering antiBlack racism
abs: Research has widely recognized antiBlackness as a particular form of white supremacy, denouncing its normalization of systemic harm across multiple domains of life for Black communities. Particularly, white supremacy standardizes the racialization of Black students and professionals through racialized speech, practices, and spaces, even within progressive schools, universities, and educational organizations. This study illuminates how in spaces that ostensibly reject antiBlackness, white supremacy persists both discursively and institutionally, offering a critical insight into the semiotic and rhetorical maneuvers that characterize narratives of countering antiBlack racism (CABR). Our investigation focused on conversations between stakeholders of a state-affiliated organization whose mission centers around multilingual advocacy to uncover standardized protocols and actors that perpetuate racialized ideologies. Drawing from critical discourse analysis, we examined the organization’s CABR committee podcast episodes, which featured a committee member as host and organizational board members as guests. Findings revealed a novel and nuanced continuum of discursive moves that encompass general dispositions toward CABR, ‘Emerging into CABR,’ ‘Grappling with CABR,’ and ‘Enacting CABR,’ that underscore significant implications for applied and sociolinguistics theory, research, and practice.

t: ‘We want white native speakers from the UK’: native speakerism in ELT course books for young learners
abs: Despite the importance of course books (CBs) in English Language Teaching (ELT) and numerous studies showing discriminatory native speakerist hiring policies in ELT, only two studies exist on how native speakerism can affect the hiring of course book authors (CBAs), and none on CBs for young learners. This study is thus the first to investigate the representation of ‘native speakers’, ‘non-native speakers’, white people, and people of colour (POC) as CBAs in internationally published CBs for young learners by six global publishers. Using native speakerism as the main theoretical framework, the study showed that 90 per cent of the CBAs were ‘native speakers’ and 96 per cent were white, and 67 per cent from the UK. Moreover, 74 per cent of the CBs were exclusively authored by ‘native speakers’ and 86 per cent by white authors, with a clear preference for CBAs from the UK (67 per cent). Potential explanations for this lack of diversity include homophilous hiring, colour-blindness, and market pressure. The study highlights the need for systemic changes in hiring policies to promote diversity and inclusion, such as open calls for authors, concrete diversity goals, and double-blind application processes.

t: Prosodic encoding and the development of durable lexical representations in L2 English: a randomised controlled longitudinal study
abs: Robust L2 lexical representations require not only semantic and orthographic knowledge but also precise phonological specification, yet the role of lexical stress remains underexplored. Intermediate Arab EFL learners (n = 132) were cluster-randomized to either a Prosodic Encoding Group, receiving a multi-cue encoding package with explicit stress-perception and stress-production activities, or an Active Control Group, receiving meaning-focused vocabulary instruction without systematic stress emphasis. Participants learned forty mid- to low-frequency academic words over six weeks. Outcome measures included immediate and delayed retention tests, timed lexical decision tasks, controlled written and oral production tasks, stress perception assessments and acoustic production analysis. Linear mixed-effects models and multilevel mediation analyses were employed. The Prosodic Encoding Group demonstrated superior delayed retention with medium-to-large effects (ds ≈ 0.8–1.1), faster lexical retrieval and higher productive accuracy. Stress perception gains were statistically associated with delayed retention, consistent with a role for suprasegmental specification in lexical durability. These findings support integrating prosodically oriented, multi-cue training within L2 vocabulary instruction, while acknowledging that stress specification’s unique contribution was not isolated from other prosodic and multimodal supports.

t: Identifying communicative needs and real-world tasks for EFL agriculture students: a task-based needs analysis
abs: Task-based language teaching (TBLT) aims to prepare learners for real-world tasks, which can be identified through task-based needs analysis (TBNA). TBNA is especially relevant in specialized study programmes with clear language demands, such as agriculture-related programmes for English learners. However, the real-world tasks these learners must perform remain underexplored, as existing studies often rely on linguistic or text-based analyses, underscoring the need for further TBNA research. This study uses a TBNA to explore the communicative needs and target tasks of English as foreign language agriculture students in Chile. It focuses on tasks requiring English in technicians’ jobs and examines perspectives from key professionals. The study employed qualitative data collection, including twenty-three interviews and document analysis. Participants included ten technicians, two managers, and eleven teachers. Findings revealed two main communicative needs and twenty-three target tasks students are likely to perform in the L2 in the target situation, revealing gaps in their English education. The study demonstrates the value of TBNA for triangulated task identification and offers insights for curriculum developers and teachers selecting tasks in TBLT. It also advances TBNA research and presents a framework transferable to similar contexts.

t: The epistemic affordance of experiential knowledge: a case study of descriptions of personal experiences with beauty supplements
abs: Experiential knowledge has persuasive effects in the communication and dissemination of health knowledge. Research has shown that anecdotes and personal stories are common in health communication despite their subjectivity and under-representativeness, but detailed discourse analysis of their pragmatic effects remains scarce. This paper presents a case study examining the discursive construction of knowledge about beauty-enhancing supplements. It analyzes online comments on the popular Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu using Discursive Psychology. The results show that the inherent evidentiality of descriptions of personal experiences contributes to their communicative affordance for constructing reliable knowledge. The use of such descriptions to achieve other social practices presupposes and demonstrates that they can be recognized and used as valid knowledge, though not without limitations. In doing so, commentators are positioned as rational, accountable sources of knowledge rather than as biased or authoritative figures on the topic. The findings also suggest a potential reconciliation between scientific and experiential knowledge, with the latter complementing rather than competing with the former.

t: The role of teacher gaze in speaking turns during interactive book reading: a multiple case mobile-eye-tracking study
abs: Gaze is foregrounded as a central interactional resource positioning individuals as speakers or bystanders. In early childhood education (ECE), where direct involvement in interactions with the teacher is central to language development and where unequal participation may lay the groundwork for far-reaching processes of educational inequality, research into gaze remains scarce. This study, including six teachers and thirty children, examines variation in children’s involvement during book reading activities and analyses how teachers shape these conversational dynamics. Using epistemic network analysis alongside multimodal quantitative and qualitative conversation analyses, this study provides a fine-grained account of multimodal turn-taking. The findings reveal unequal distribution of teacher attention, resulting in unequal opportunities for children to participate. Results revealed a relationship between teachers’ fixations (i.e. sustained moments of visual attention) and both teachers’ and children’s speaking turns, underscoring the central importance of gaze in conversational dynamics in classrooms. Conversation analysis further shows that children’s participation is largely teacher-driven, with most child turns being initiated by the teacher. Overall, the results indicate interactional inequalities in ECE.

t: The Experience of Expatriate English Language Teaching
The Language Teacher Education Casebook
INTRODUCING SECOND LANGUAGE ASSESSMENT
The Country in the voice: resonance, language, and belonging after displacement
abs: Research in applied linguistics shows that first languages differ from later-learned languages in prosodic, physiological, and emotional processing, shaping affective expression and interpersonal regulation. Yet these findings are rarely connected to questions of belonging and displacement. This article brings research in phonetics, bilingualism, and affective neuroscience into dialogue with Indigenous relational ontology to examine voice and mother tongue as embodied carriers of belonging. The article argues that language functions not only as a system of meaning but also as a regulatory signal shaped through early relational experience. First languages are spoken with distinct patterns of intonation, rhythm, and vocal effort, reflecting deeper embodiment and affective attunement. When displacement or assimilation marginalizes the mother tongue, the resulting disruption is not only cultural or symbolic, but physiological and relational. Drawing on the Indigenous concept of Kanyini, the article conceptualizes voice as a portable form of relational grounding and discusses implications for applied linguistics in contexts of migration, education, trauma, and multilingual family life.

t: Research Methods for Applied Linguistics: A Practical Guide
A revised model of feedback-seeking behavior in SLA: toward improved conceptualization and measurement
abs: This study proposed and tested a revised model of feedback-seeking behavior in second language acquisition. The revised model included feedback elicitation, monitoring, and use. In two studies, data were collected from 207 learners enrolled in Spanish classes at a large public university in Florida and 294 learners of English at a multi-branch private language institute in Iran. Exploratory factor analyses generally combined CF Monitoring and CF Use, whereas confirmatory factor analyses favored the hypothesized three-factor model, with stronger support in Study 2. The scales demonstrated acceptable convergent validity and internal consistency, although the distinction between Monitoring and Use was limited in Study 1 and improved in Study 2. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses further showed that the overall FSB index significantly predicted self-assessed L2 proficiency in both contexts, although the unique contributions of the individual components varied across samples. Overall, the findings supported the tripartite model of FSB, defined as learners’ proactive efforts to elicit, monitor, and use CF to enhance their L2 production. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed, and future research directions are outlined.

t: Foreign language learner well-being: operationalization and validation of the E4MC model
abs: With the growing interest in foreign language (FL) learner well-being, there is an increased need for solid holistic models that have a strong theoretical foundation and instruments that are both economical and reliable. The present study proposes an operationalization and psychometric validation of the newly developed hierarchical E4MC model as a multidimensional structural model comprising interconnected building blocks of language learner well-being. E4MC consists of six lenses, namely emotions, empathy, engagement, emotional intelligence, motivation, and character strengths. The new seventy-three-item instrument was tested with data collected online from 328 FL learners from different parts of the world. Measurement models for each of the six lenses were found to be satisfactory. A parcelled structural equation model revealed strong inter-relations between the lenses. Finally, latent models were shown to have a good fit. We conclude that the newly developed instrument does provide researchers with a valid tool to measure FL learner well-being.

t: Evaluating large language models with tests of Spanish as a foreign language: pass or fail?
abs: Large language models (LLMs) have been profusely evaluated on their ability to answer questions on many topics and their performance on different natural language understanding tasks. Those tests are usually conducted in English, but most LLM users are not native English speakers. Therefore, it is of interest to analyse how LLMs understand other languages at different levels: from paragraphs to morphemes. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art LLMs in TELEIA, a recently released benchmark with similar questions to those of Spanish exams for foreign students, covering topics such as reading comprehension, word formation, meaning and compositional semantics, and grammar. The results show that LLMs perform well at understanding Spanish but are still far from achieving the level of a native speaker in terms of grammatical competence.

t: Adaptable English Language Teaching: Advances and Frameworks for Responding to New Circumstances
Hablo pocha, ¿no?: divergent language ideologies of pocho and mocho at the U.S.–Mexico border
abs: Language ideologies of linguistic purism in the U.S.–Mexico borderlands have long produced pejorative labels for bilingual practices used among Mexican Americans, including pocho and mocho. Although these terms appear frequently in research on U.S. Spanish, little is known about how bilinguals themselves use and interpret them. This study provides the first corpus-based analysis of pocho/mocho across two border regions—South Texas and Southern Arizona—drawing on 184 sociolinguistic interviews. Monoglossic stances frame pocho/mocho as speaking a language improperly, as incorrect or aesthetically undesirable, or as harming the language(s). In contrast, heteroglossic stances revalue these terms as markers of solidarity, identity, linguistic pride, and culturally meaningful communicative practices at the border. Using a raciolinguistic and stance-based framework, the analysis shows that speakers mobilize these labels to index multiple, sometimes contradictory ideologies. These findings demonstrate that pocho/mocho operate as dynamic ideological tools through which speakers police, negotiate, and reclaim bilingualism. The study also highlights implications for education, Spanish for the professions, and language-access efforts in the borderlands.

t: ‘I call myself a five (rubbish/loser), but I don’t really want to be’: online identity and translanguaging play in social media
abs: Failure or being a loser are identities not openly recognized or acceptable in a merit-driven society, especially for top university students. This study investigates the role of translanguaging play in negotiating identities related to precarious life experiences within a Chinese online community on Douban. Drawing on discourse-centered online ethnography (DCOE) and Moment Analysis, we explore how ‘loser’ identities are negotiated, destabilized, and subverted through homophonic wordplay on ‘five’. The findings reveal that participants employ translanguaging play to reclaim the ‘five’ label in self-deprecation, develop ‘five lexicology’ to build solidarity, and oscillate between ‘being a five’ and ‘de-fiving’ under meritocratic pressures. These demonstrate participants’ creativity in deploying diverse semiotic resources alongside metalinguistic and genre knowledge. We further argue that psychological distance between named languages itself constitutes a translanguaging resource for identity work, as the affective gap between English five and Chinese fèiwù (rubbish/loser) enables participants to re-represent failure through a register of playful lightness. Translanguaging play thus carves out a safe space in which vulnerability can be voiced, ascribed identities transcended, and resilience cultivated against uncertainty.

t: Multi-word expressions and communicative engagement: A longitudinal study of L2 learners’ willingness to communicate
abs: Despite growing interest in willingness to communicate (WTC) in second language (L2) research, the role of multi-word expressions (MWEs) in fostering communicative engagement remains underexplored. This longitudinal mixed-methods study examines the impact of MWEs on WTC development among L2 learners. Over twelve months, seventy-seven intermediate-level learners participated in an experimental design where MWE knowledge and WTC were assessed at five time points. The experimental group (n = 58) received explicit MWE instruction, while the control group (n = 19) followed the standard curriculum. Data collection included WTC scales, MWE recall tests, structured classroom observations, and learner interviews. For the MWEs and WTC data, mixed ANOVA and hierarchical regression modeling were used to test whether MWE gains predict WTC increases; and for the observation data, descriptive statistics were utilized. Qualitative data were also analyzed through thematic coding. Quantitative analyses revealed that MWE gains significantly predicted increases in WTC over time. Qualitative findings corroborated these results, showing that MWEs enhanced communicative confidence and encouraged risk-taking. The study underscored the need for integrating MWEs into L2 instruction to foster greater communicative engagement.

t: Grounded Theory in Applied Linguistics Research: A Practical Guide (Second Edition)
Measuring speaker intent and awareness in language-discordant communication: the communication accommodation behavior scale
abs: When people share a language but differ in proficiency, higher proficiency speakers often adjust their speech for lower proficiency listeners. They might speak slower, simplify sentence structures, or use exaggerated articulation to support understanding and manage social dynamics. Speech accommodation across proficiencies (LX accommodation) can improve comprehension when it meets the needs of the lower proficiency speaker. However, it is not yet clear how a speaker’s accommodation behavior relates to their attitudes about accommodation, or how empathy, anxiety, and language experience influence accommodation attitudes. We developed the Communication Accommodation Behavior Scale (CABS) to assess two dimensions of this relationship: positive, prosocial intent (i.e. “Facilitative Accommodation”) and negative feelings, including avoidance (i.e. “Resistant Accommodation”). A representative sample of English-speaking (L1) participants (n = 525) completed the eight-item CABS, surveys of empathy and anxiety, and a demographic and language experience questionnaire. A factor analysis revealed a two-factor CABS structure, supporting its utility for research purposes. Age, experience abroad, and interpersonal empathy influenced CABS scores, revealing complex individual differences in accommodation strategies linked to experience and stable personality traits.

t: The impact of L2 learners’ use of AI on their grit, shyness, and L2 achievements
abs: This study looked at the long-term impact of the use of artificial intelligence (AI) on the grit, shyness, and overall language achievements of L2 English learners at different levels of proficiency. A total of 122 Korean university students participated in the study. The three research instruments consisted of L2 grit and shyness scales, the Test of English for International Communication (TOEIC), and focus group interviews. The results indicated that the learners increased their L2 grit levels and TOEIC scores and decreased their shyness levels because of the rise in AI use. Of the proficiency groups, the intermediate level group’s increases/decreases were the greatest. Further, these changes were significant. Based on the findings of the study, implications are suggested.

t: Precarity in an adult refugee’s basic literacy learning
abs: With this article, we respond to recent calls within research on language learning for a greater focus on societal impact by drawing attention to the needs of different learner groups. We are concerned with a group of learners who have received limited attention in the field: adult refugees with limited prior schooling who enter graphocentric spaces. Language learning is often an inevitability for this group. For instance, in Norway, where our research was carried out, Norwegian language training is juridically ‘a right and an obligation’ for refugees. This article is an ethnographic case study of the basic literacy learning of Nora, a resettlement refugee from the DR Congo via Uganda to Norway. Our main finding is that there was a large gap between Nora’s priorities and understandings—informed by her refugee trajectory—and the aims and content of the basic literacy training she attended during her first years in Norway. Based on Nora’s story, we argue that the precarity of the refugee condition should be addressed, to better understand refugees’ needs as language learners.

t: APPLICATIONS OF CORPUS LINGUISTICS: ESTABLISHED AND EMERGENT CONTEXTS
DISMANTLING THE NATIVE SPEAKER CONSTRUCT IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING
Ten years of translanguaging: reflections and future directions in dialogue with Ofelia García and Li Wei
abs: Marking a decade since the publication of Translanguaging: Language, Bilingualism, and Education, this forum revisits the evolution of translanguaging as a theoretical, pedagogical, and sociopolitical framework. Drawing on a dialogue with Ofelia García and Li Wei, the discussion reflects on how translanguaging has reshaped understandings of multilingualism, language education, and linguistic justice across diverse contexts. The exchange examines the conceptual development of translanguaging, its uneven institutional uptake across Global North and Global South settings, and its implications for pedagogy, teacher education, and language policy. It also considers the emerging challenges posed by digital technologies and artificial intelligence for multilingual knowledge production and classroom practice. The forum highlights the importance of critically engaging with translanguaging’s epistemological foundations while remaining attentive to local sociolinguistic conditions and structural inequalities. In doing so, it outlines key directions for translanguaging research and practice in the coming decade.

t: Social perception of English irony: a comparison of L1 and L2 speakers
abs: Irony plays an important role in social communication, but its perceived politeness and appropriateness can vary across linguistic backgrounds. This study investigated how first-language (L1) English speakers and advanced second-language (L2) English speakers (Chinese L1) evaluate ironic (sarcastic, teasing) versus literal statements in audio-visual conversations. Participants watched videos and rated them on politeness, appropriateness, and their own likelihood of using them. Stimuli differed by communicative intent (positive vs. negative) and delivery style (literal vs. ironic). Both groups judged literal and positive statements as more polite and appropriate than ironic and negative ones. However, L1 and L2 speakers differed in how willing they were to use irony themselves, with L1 speakers preferring literal over ironic remarks more strongly than L2 speakers. Sarcastic remarks were judged less polite than literal negative statements, contrary to predictions of the Tinge Hypothesis that irony softens criticism. Our findings show that paralinguistic cues shape irony evaluation and that L2 speakers interpret irony similarly to L1 speakers but are more cautious about using it themselves. These results advance the understanding of intercultural pragmatics and L2 sociopragmatic development.

t: Rethinking language learning motivation through a dialogic lens
abs: Conventional studies on second language (L2) motivation have often emphasized two key concepts: integrativeness and the ideal L2 self. While each offers valuable insight, they are typically treated as distinct psychological processes, and neither concept alone may sufficiently account for the diverse nature of motivation. This study argues that this limitation stems from the field’s reliance on Saussurean linguistics, which views language learning as the internalization of linguistic knowledge. To address this, Bakhtin’s dialogism is employed, framing language learning as a dialogic process involving the appropriation of others’ words. Using dialogism as a framework, the motivations of two learners of Japanese were examined. Analysis of interview data revealed that the learners’ engagement in actual and imagined Japanese dialogues within various social communications evolved and deepened over time, centering on their appropriation of specific speech genres historically used in these communications. The findings suggest that integrativeness and the ideal L2 self share a common process of identification with the target language and can coexist within the same dialogic process situated in particular forms of social communication.

t: Vocabulary structure in foreign language learners: a complex network analysis perspective
abs: This empirical study explores the vocabulary structure of heritage minority learners of English as a foreign language (EFL) within a Spanish mainstream educational context. Using graph analysis and complex network theory, the study examines lexical organization among learners of local origin (Spanish monolinguals) and heritage multilingual learners from Arabic, Romanian, and Urdu backgrounds. Results reveal no significant quantitative differences in lexical production among groups, but qualitative distinctions in lexical-semantic structures emerge. Heritage learners exhibit vocabulary networks influenced by their linguistic and cultural backgrounds, with distinct cluster formations compared to local learners. Small-world properties characterize all lexical networks, indicating efficient word retrieval structures. Findings highlight the role of schooling in standardizing vocabulary acquisition while cultural and linguistic experiences shape lexical access patterns. The study underscores the need for plurilingual approaches in EFL education to accommodate diverse linguistic backgrounds.

t: Task complexity and genre effects: examining complexity, accuracy, and fluency in L2 oral production
abs: While genre-related second language (L2) research has primarily focused on written production and isolated linguistic dimensions, limited attention has been paid to how genre modulates task complexity and linguistic performance in L2 oral contexts. Grounded in two theoretical frameworks—the limited attentional capacity model and the cognition hypothesis—this study investigates how expository and narrative genres influence the complexity, accuracy, and fluency of L2 oral performance. College-level English learners completed two 60-second speaking tasks: one expository and one narrative. The results showed that expository responses exhibited higher lexical diversity, more sophisticated vocabulary, and greater syntactic complexity compared to narrative responses. However, these gains in complexity were accompanied by trade-offs, including reduced accuracy in segmental pronunciation and grammar, as well as diminished prosodic fluency. While these findings align with previous research on genre effects in L2 writing, the pronounced trade-offs observed in speaking highlight how real-time processing demands exacerbate cognitive constraints.

t: The (un)coupling of language and race in a Green Mong teacher’s advocacy for dialect equity
abs: This case study explores Xee, a bilingual Hmong teacher’s observed dialect inequity at her dual language bilingual education (DLBE) program and advocacy through a LangCrit lens. Multiple interviews and informal conversations were utilized to gain an understanding of Xee’s critical consciousness for the inclusion of the Green Mong dialect within the Hmong-English DLBE. The findings reveal that the strict boundaries between the two dialects, Green Mong and White Hmong, were socially constructed and imposed through specific strategies that both ascribed an assumed and imposed identity of White Hmong onto Green Mong students and a linguistic hierarchy at the DLBE. Xee’s advocacy efforts aimed at providing students with a third space to negotiate their Green Mong identity while also othering/racializing parents and teachers against a White norm. In the discussion and conclusion sections, I recommend that a critical stance should also be extended to parents and families to avoid deficit identities and stereotypes, and call for more investigation into inequitable conditions in one-way DLBE programs.

t: AI and the simplification of task design
abs: This commentary begins by summarizing Jeon et al.’s (2025) concerns about Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)’s tendency to standardize language, followed by Hu’s (2026) response, on how to bring Artificial Intelligence (AI) into teaching (academic) writing in ways that allow for negotiation of forms. My own response, given the bigger picture, is whether AI needs to be used at all. First, as a former English for Academic Purposes (EAP) writing instructor, I argue that AI represents writing tasks differently from humans, and that going along with its simplified representation is a step back after human experts have rendered more complex representations of the tasks. Second, as a qualitative researcher, I argue that AI is of limited use in qualitative data analysis, since what qualitative researchers analyze goes beyond what is in the text. I conclude that in both these cases, AI simplifies tasks and detracts from what students of academic writing or novice qualitative researchers need to learn.

t: Understanding second language student engagement with digital multimodal composing
abs: While the effectiveness of digital multimodal composing (DMC) has garnered growing scholarly attention within the field of applied linguistics, little is known about how second language students engage with DMC to improve learning and writing. Conceptualizing student engagement with DMC as a tripartite construct, this qualitative case study examined two triad groups (one highly-engaged and the other minimally-engaged) of undergraduates’ behavioral, cognitive, and affective engagement with collaborative DMC in a Chinese EFL classroom. Data were collected from various sources, including students’ DMC drafts, stimulated recalls, semi-structured interviews, and classroom documents. The analysis revealed notable variations in student engagement levels between the two groups, as evidenced by their behavioral allocation of time and revision activities, application of cognitive strategies, and emotional responses to multimodal creation. Our findings underscore student engagement with DMC as an interconnected system influenced by a complex interplay of individual and contextual factors. The current study contributes to our understanding of the under-explored construct of student engagement with DMC, offering useful implications for DMC pedagogical practices and further research.

t: Abnormal deceivers? Biopower in clinician accounts of embodiment and life for people with intersex variations
abs: This research underscores the power of direct clinician–patient interaction to both reproduce and disrupt biopolitical paradigms, offering insights for improving practice and policy in our responses to intersex variations. I examine how clinicians in Hong Kong give accounts of their professional talk about intersex variations of innate sex characteristics, foregrounding the role of language in shaping medical decision-making and biopower in healthcare. Drawing on interactional sociolinguistics, I show via close analysis of in-depth interviews the stancetaking processes through which interviewed clinicians negotiate social, institutional, and personal ideologies regarding intersex variations. I identify deficit and non-deficit framings in the accounts, with attention to gender, ableism, and cultural norms inflecting how embodiment is reportedly discussed with patients and families. By situating the findings within the Hong Kong context, the article challenges Western-centric theoretical models and demonstrates the global relevance of applied linguistics in healthcare settings. I explicate how language choices contribute to patient understanding and agency, the perpetuation or contestation of binary gender norms, and the broader management of bodily diversity.

t: Shaping an enduring conversation on AI in applied linguistics
Doing Vocabulary Research by Elke Peters (Routledge, New York, 2025)
abs: Vocabulary is an essential building block of language. Given its central role, the past two decades have witnessed a remarkable surge in vocabulary studies, yielding substantial insights into how words are learned, processed, and used by second language (L2) learners, many of which hold direct implications for instructional practice. However, the promise of these insights hinges on the robustness of relevant studies in terms of methodological rigor, transparency, and replicability. Even innovative findings can falter if the methodology is flawed or reports lack transparency. This underscores the need for methodological rigor and transparency (Plonsky 2024). In this context, Elke Peters’s Doing Vocabulary Research stands out as a highly anticipated contribution, offering a comprehensive roadmap for navigating the various methodological options of L2 vocabulary research. As a prominent scholar with more than two decades of sustained engagement in the field, Peters writes from an insider perspective that lends the book both credibility and practical depth. She situates this work within the field’s rich intellectual traditions through references to foundational works, while positioning this volume as an up-to-date account of current developments. The book is organized around four themes to ensure accessibility: an overview of L2 vocabulary research (Chapter 1), vocabulary assessment (Chapters 2–5), research designs (Chapters 6–11), and a forward-looking reflection on future directions (Chapter 12).

t: L2 grit unboxed: A meta-analytic journey into L2 grit and its correlates
abs: As an emerging field of study within second language acquisition (SLA), the notion of grit has gained immediate relevance as it is considered to play a key role in language achievement. Although recent years have witnessed increasing attention to second language (L2) grit due to its merits in foreign/second language learning processes, a comprehensive meta-analysis synthesizing the results of all available studies on the relationship between L2 grit and its frequently associated variables is currently lacking. Therefore, the current meta-analytic study scrutinized the total mean correlation between L2 grit and six main correlates examined in the research domain: foreign language enjoyment, L2 motivation, foreign language anxiety (FLA), ideal L2 self, growth mindset, and teacher support. A total of k = 34 effect sizes were analyzed with an overall sample size of N = 13,068 in random-effects models with correlation coefficients. The findings indicated that L2 motivation is the strongest correlate of L2 grit (r = .58), indicating a large effect size. The other five variables were moderately correlated with L2 grit, with FLA (r = −.47) being the strongest correlate and growth mindset (r = .33) being the weakest correlate. Implications of these findings and directions for future research are discussed.

t: A longitudinal examination of psychological capital and academic achievement in EMI courses: A multivariate latent growth curve modeling approach
abs: With English Medium Instruction (EMI) expanding in China’s higher education, understanding the psychological factors supporting student success is essential. This study examines how psychological capital (PsyCap), comprising self-efficacy, hope, resilience, and optimism, relates to academic achievement over time. Using the Psychological Capital Scale for EMI Learners (PsyCap-EMI) and multivariate latent growth curve modeling, data were collected from 489 Chinese EFL students in EMI courses at four time points across 2 years. Results showed that PsyCap gradually increased over time. Higher initial PsyCap predicted stronger initial academic achievement (β = 0.54). The initial level of PsyCap was negatively correlated with subsequent growth in psychological resources (r = −0.25). Additionally, initial PsyCap was negatively linked to academic growth (β = −0.20), while PsyCap increases were positively but weakly related to academic improvement (β = 0.12). Qualitative interviews further revealed fluctuations in students’ psychological states and academic experiences. The findings highlight the dynamic role of PsyCap in EMI learning and underscore the need for institutional strategies that foster psychological development alongside academic support in linguistically demanding contexts.

t: Learner Language, Discourse and Interaction: A Corpus-Based Analysis of Spoken English
abs: Learner language research has long been central to second language acquisition (SLA) and applied linguistics, serving as a bridge between SLA, corpus linguistics, and pedagogy (Gilquin and Granger 2015; Tracy-Ventura and Paquot 2021). Yet the field has historically suffered from a “written language bias” (Linell 2004), privileging accuracy and lexical knowledge while marginalizing spoken interaction. This imbalance—partly attributable to the relative ease of compiling written corpora compared with the labor-intensive construction of spoken corpora (Randi 2010; McEnery and Brookes 2022)—has limited the ecological validity of SLA and obscured the dynamics of authentic learner–native speaker interaction (Gilmore 2007). Against this backdrop, Learner Language, Discourse and Interaction: A Corpus-Based Analysis of Spoken English offers a novel perspective. Drawing on the Trinity Lancaster Corpus (TLC), its L1 counterpart, and the Spoken BNC2014, the book presents the first large-scale, corpus-based analysis of discourse macro-structures in L1–L2 spoken interaction. Together, these corpora provide a dual comparative framework—L2 versus L1 and examination versus everyday settings—enabling the authors to disentangle the effects of proficiency, task, and context, while extending learner corpus research into more ecologically valid domains (Curry and McEnery 2025). Methodologically, the volume applies short-text multi-dimensional analysis (MDA; Biber 1988; Friginal and Weigle 2014; Clarke 2022), linking co-occurring linguistic features to communicative functions, and situates MDA within a transparent, data-driven analytical framework (McEnery and Brezina 2022).

t: Individual Network of Linguistic Practice (INoLP): Quantifying social networks and pragmatic competence of international students during their sojourn abroad
abs: Study abroad (SA) programs are widely recognized for their role in enhancing students’ language skills through immersive environments. However, there remains a gap in understanding how social interaction within these contexts influences their pragmatic development. This study examines the relationship between international students’ social networks and their pragmatic competence, introducing a novel individual network of linguistic practice (INoLP) framework to conceptualize language use and interactions in SA settings. Appropriateness judgment tasks were administered to 311 Chinese international students in the UK to measure their receptive pragmatic competence. Their social networks were mapped using a graphical interactive questionnaire. Quantitative analysis revealed significant correlations between pragmatic competence and several social network properties, including size, similarity, the presence of L2-speaking interlocutors, tie strength, contact frequency, and tie dispersion. Moreover, four network properties—tie dispersion, tie strength with multinationals, contact frequency with conationals, and the presence of L2-speaking contacts—emerged as significant predictors of pragmatic competence. This study pioneers a quantitative exploration of pragmatic competence through a social network lens, offering insights with theoretical, methodological, and practical implications.

t: Revealing the complex system of self-regulation strategies, achievement emotions, and L2 grit in online English learning
abs: This study advances our understanding of the complex interplay of self-regulated learning (SRL) strategies, achievement emotions, and second language (L2) grit in online English learning from a complex systems perspective. A cohort of 263 Chinese non-English majors completed self-report questionnaires once they finished a 16-week online English course. Using psychological network analysis (PNA), a novel method for exploring psycho-emotional traits within a unified network, this study mapped the interrelationships among cognitive (SRL strategies), affective (achievement emotions), and personality (L2 grit) factors across different proficiency levels. The PNA results confirmed complex interrelationships among these individual factors and revealed SRL strategies emerging as the most central variables interacting with achievement emotions (hope, hopelessness, enjoyment, and boredom) and L2 grit. Furthermore, network comparison tests identified significant differences between the high and low proficiency groups in three interrelationships: motivational regulation strategies-hopelessness, cognitive strategies-L2 grit, and enjoyment-L2 grit. These findings extend SRL theory by unveiling the interconnectedness of strategies, emotions, and personality in online environments and issue a call for humanistic, learner-centered L2 education.

t: Challenging assumptions about migrant language use: Evidence from a Swedish study with the Experience Sampling Method and the Lang-Track-App
abs: In an era of global migration, where public discourse often assumes that migrants lack exposure to and command of local majority language(s), it is a crucial research task to understand how migrants learn and use new languages in their everyday lives. This study provides empirical evidence about the quantity and nature of everyday language exposure and use (LEU) among migrants in Sweden. Using the Experience Sampling Method and the Lang-Track-App, we collected rich self-report data across three weeks from 45 adult migrants with diverse backgrounds. Group-level quantitative analyses revealed that, despite considerable individual variation and occasional linguistic challenges, Swedish was the most used language across a broad range of self-reported daily activities. Complementary qualitative analysis of two cases illustrated the nuanced and fluctuating nature of LEU, which did not align predictably with structural factors such as employment, student status, or social networks. Instead, LEU appeared to emerge through dynamic interplay between individual agency and contextual affordances. These findings challenge prevailing narratives about migrants’ limited contact with the majority language and underscore the value of capturing LEU through temporally and contextually sensitive methods.

t: Epistemologies of language and epistemic injustice in adult basic education for immigrants
abs: Many adults who immigrate from the Global South to Western countries experience devaluation of their knowledge and expertise. Such epistemic injustice may be exacerbated by Eurocentric epistemologies of language as fixed and codified, rather than as a dynamic, relational practice. This study explores how these dynamics unfold in adult basic education by examining intersections of language and epistemic injustice, including hermeneutical, contributory, and testimonial injustice. Drawing on ethnographic data from a collaborative translanguaging project in Norway, we show how (1) dominant institutional conceptions of language created interpretive gaps obscuring students’ epistemic resources (hermeneutical injustice); (2) teachers often misrecognized students’ linguistic expertise, both form-focused and practice-oriented, based on legibility problems in their classroom practices (contributory injustice); and (3) institutional placement procedures underestimated students’ educational qualifications and language skills through a monolanguaging mode of listening (testimonial injustice). We call for interlinked first-, second-, and third-order change to institutional practices, modes of perception, and forms of relationality, underscoring that multilingual pedagogies must explicitly commit to epistemic equality if they are to counter, rather than reproduce, entrenched inequalities.

t: Institutional “lingualism” as an interactional achievement: A sequential typology of initial language access
abs: This paper seeks to expand our understanding of mono-, bi-, and multi-lingualism through a comparative analysis across social institutions. First, we explore some of the concrete interactional practices used by institutions to enact and promote—or resist and impede—the use of different languages with members of the public. Examining data from three distinct organizations in the southwestern USA, here we ask: What does it take—interactionally—to be able to use Spanish in a given institutional context? Moving beyond claims that Spanish is “available,” what interactional work do members of society in fact have to put in to access it? Our second objective is then to offer a sequential typology of different procedural means through which language is accessed in these different institutions. Distinctions are made between what we call “proferred bilingualism,” “acquiesced bilingualism,” and “reluctant bilingualism,” as well as “coerced monolingualism,” on the part of institutions. The practice-based, comparative approach exemplified here, grounded in the details of moment-by-moment talk, is used to introduce the notion of institutional lingualism more broadly, and lay the foundations for future (critical) exploration of just how mono-/bi-/multi-lingual social institutions are, in actual practice.

t: ‘I’m a Latina with an Asian body’: Authenticating ethnolinguistic identities amid raciolinguistic and monolingual ideologies
abs: This qualitative study, grounded in LangCrit, language ideologies, and third space theory, analyzes autobiographical interviews with eighteen Spanish-speaking, US-based Latin Asians—individuals of Latin American and Asian heritage. Participants describe how the co-naturalization of mestizaje, Spanish, and latinidad often excludes them from being recognized as Latine or Latin American, or as native or heritage Spanish speakers, because of their racial appearance. Simultaneously, they confront expectations to know their Asian heritage language(s), often judged against idealized monolingual and monocultural standards. These competing demands limit their identity possibilities. In response, participants mobilize semiotic and multilingual resources to construct a third space where identities can be expressed beyond binary categories. Findings reveal that when phenotype restricts individuals’ access to desired ethnic identities, language becomes a powerful tool for identity reclamation, even when doing so reinforces essentialist ideologies. This study contributes to understandings of how mixed-heritage individuals navigate identities and ideologies in a sociopolitical landscape shaped by multiscalar, monoracial and monolingual norms and calls for critical awareness that challenges the conflation of language, race, and identity.

t: Bridging voices: Rethinking feedback for heritage learners in the age of artificial intelligence
Unequal trajectories? An examination of L2 development in a higher education context in Mexico
abs: Understanding how second language (L2) proficiency develops in instructional settings remains a central concern within applied linguistics. This two-year longitudinal study examines English language development in a higher education context in Mexico, addressing key methodological and empirical gaps. We tracked L2 development—operationalized as changes in the TOEFL ITP® scores—across three time points and examined a wide range of variables, including the often-neglected factor of socio-economic status (SES). Results from linear mixed effects modelling and sensitivity analyses showed statistically significant, though small, gains in proficiency. Baseline proficiency emerged as a strong predictor of learning trajectories, with lower-proficiency students showing greater relative improvement. SES, contact with English, and age of onset were the most consistent predictors of L2 performance. Mediation analysis indicated that SES influences proficiency both directly and indirectly, primarily through contact with English. However, much of the SES effect remained unexplained, suggesting broader systemic influences. These findings shed light on hidden disparities in language education and offer insights for educational policy, highlighting the need to address structural barriers to equitable L2 development.
k: Test of English as a Foreign Language

t: Investigating transpositioning as an interactional achievement: Expanding the promise of membership categorization analysis
abs: In social interaction, we take on and are ascribed multiplex social categories. The capacity to transform, transcend, and transgress the boundaries of categories is the ability to transposition, a necessity for thriving in social life in the 21st century. This paper has two related goals. Theoretically, it argues that transpositioning is an interactional achievement and to understand this process, one needs to inspect on a moment-by-moment basis how speakers move beyond confines of their social categories. Methodologically, it extends the promise of Membership Categorization Analysis and posits that when employed in conjunction with sequential analysis through Conversation Analysis, it illuminates how transpositioning takes place at an interactional level. We present our arguments through analyses of transpositioning processes in three distinct language use contexts: workplace, everyday and educational interactions. In addition to conceptual and methodological contributions, the paper sheds light on the relationship between transpositioning and the morality of interaction, the emancipatory potential of transpositioning practices, and the connection between transpositioning on shorter and longer timescales. Implications for pedagogy and human-AI interactions are also discussed.

t: Pedagogical translanguaging with GenAI: From dilemmas to design
abs: This article revisits the dilemmas of creativity–standardization, inclusion–fixity, and meaning–form, as proposed by Jeon et al. (2025), in relation to the intersection of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) within translanguaging. While their contribution centers on a mechanism-level analysis of the input–output asymmetry of large language models, I adopt a pedagogical perspective and argue that these dilemmas remain pertinent in the context of pedagogical translanguaging. However, they may not always apply in the same way across classroom settings, particularly when standardization, fixity, and form are not inherently problematic and are instead intentionally calibrated by educators to foster creativity, inclusion, and meaning. I therefore recast the dilemmas as questions of classroom governance rather than properties of GenAI or translanguaging, and propose a reciprocal framing–reframing approach in which pedagogical translanguaging sets the terms of GenAI’s participation and GenAI, once introduced, presses those terms to be made explicit and auditable.

t: Ethical awareness versus actual practices: Chinese doctoral students in AI-assisted academic writing
abs: Despite artificial intelligence (AI)’s transformative impact on education, empirical work on students’ ethical awareness and actual practices when navigating AI-related dilemmas remains scarce. This study examined 25 Chinese doctoral students across disciplines via an AI-assisted simulated literature review task, two qualitative surveys, and student-AI dialogues. Key findings: (1) Most demonstrated AI ethics awareness but focused on system-related concerns over self-relevant issues (e.g. eroded autonomy, blurred authorship). (2) All students used AI in at least one writing phase (literature understanding, synthesis, drafting, and editing) for one or more purposes (conceptual, rhetorical, or linguistic support). Faced with ‘disclose or not’ dilemma, most opted for partial disclosure in editable text. Individual variation was however observed in distributed agency and disclosure extent. (3) Discrepancies were identified between students’ stated ethical beliefs and actual behavior when navigating ethical dilemmas. Pedagogical implications were discussed including an advocate for creating safe havens for students to experiment AI-use and negotiate context-specific ethics.

t: Linguistic insights into Alzheimer’s disease: A bibliometric and visual analysis (1995–2024)
abs: Amidst the backdrop of global aging, the societal impact of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) has become increasingly profound. Despite the theoretical and practical value of linguistics in AD research, existing bibliometric analyses lack systematic exploration of linguistic studies in this domain. This study employs bibliometric and visual analyses to examine the development trajectory of AD linguistic research from 1995 to 2024. Findings reveal that global aging trends, policy support, and advancements in linguistic corpora have driven the non-linear growth of AD linguistic research. This study underscores the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in AD diagnosis and intervention, particularly through the integration of neuroscience, linguistics, and artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML). Core journals and high-impact publications have significantly advanced scientific discourse, although their impact remains constrained compared with broader interdisciplinary efforts. By analyzing collaboration networks among countries/regions, institutions, and authors, this study highlights the driving forces of multidisciplinary cooperation in the global research ecosystem. Future priorities include cross-cultural linguistic studies and development of AI/ML-driven tools for automated diagnostics and personalized AD care to address complex challenges.

t: English and global citizenship education: A critical examination of multilingual classrooms in the global south
abs: This study critically examines the intersection of English language teaching (ELT) and global citizenship education (GCE) in higher education (HE) through data from state-funded universities in the Global South (Colombia, Iraq, Thailand, and Vietnam). It examines how students, educators, and administrators perceive and engage with global and intercultural citizenship through the medium of English. Data were collected through 126 semi-structured interviews and analysed using thematic and content analysis to identify cross-contextual patterns and context-specific interpretations. Participants described a two-fold experience in which English facilitated global academic, professional, and personal access and mobility, while generating concerns about the erasure of local identities and knowledge systems, framed by enduring forms of epistemic inequality, cultural hierarchy, and instrumental pressures reinforced by neoliberal frameworks. In response, many educators and learners challenged dominant Anglophone models by adopting decolonial pedagogies that emphasise ethical engagement, foster critical reflexivity, and reflect locally rooted practices. The study calls for reconfiguring GCE and ELT as interconnected domains of transformation that support inclusive, context-responsive, and socially engaged models of global citizenship within Southern HE settings.

t: Unlocking the multifaceted power of self-regulated learning and generative AI in foreign language morphological skills
abs: With the advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI), foreign language (FL) education has stepped into a transformative new era. Despite the widespread usage of generative AI, understanding the role of self-regulation in micro-level language skills within generative AI-enhanced learning environments is inadequate. To address this gap, drawn on self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this study explores how mobile self-regulated learning (MSRL) affects FL learners’ generative AI awareness (optimism and dependence) and morphological skills (discrimination, interpretation, and recognition) among 614 English FL learners. The results of path analysis based on partial least squares reveal that MSRL is positively associated with both dimensions of generative AI awareness and negatively associated with the three morphological skills. The mediation analysis results reveal that the dependence dimension of generative AI awareness significantly mediates the relationship between MSRL and morphological skills (interpretation and discrimination). Contrarily, optimism does not play a mediating role. This study extends SRL theory into micro-level language skills development in AI contexts and provides pedagogical implications for designing language instruction and learning platforms in the digital era.

t: Words and meanings in cancer communication: Denotational and connotational misalignments
abs: Shared understanding of words used in cancer care is crucial to the quality of patients’ engagement with their treatment. A cancer diagnosis introduces the patient to many unfamiliar words and meanings. This study identifies words that are prone to impede communication by (i) evaluating lay participants’ (n = 292) definitional understanding of terms commonly used in cancer care and (ii) comparing the connotations of terms held by lay participants with those held by healthcare practitioners (n = 82). A critical impediment to definitional understanding was found when words are used in a different, sometimes contradictory, way from their meaning in general language use. Participants who misunderstood terms were no less confident in the accuracy of their understanding than those who understood well. Connotational meaning was assessed using semantic differential and word association techniques. A lack of congruence between lay and health practitioner connotations was found for most target terms; a substantial number of ‘fear’- or ‘sad’-related associations from lay participants contrasted with a near absence of such connotations from healthcare practitioners. Findings reveal routes to improved health communication.

t: Linguistic correlates of coherence in L2 narrative speech: a mixed-methods approach
abs: Despite growing recognition of coherence as a key indicator of functional adequacy and discourse competence in second language (L2) speaking, empirical research has rarely examined its linguistic underpinnings in spontaneous L2 speech. To address this gap, this mixed-methods study identified linguistic correlates of speech coherence in personal story generation monologues produced by seventy Chinese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. Mixed-effects modelling revealed that schematic structure and text elaboration significantly predicted expert-rated coherence with a moderate effect size. In contrast, cohesive devices, including connectives, lexical cohesion, and anaphora, were not significant predictors. Stimulated recall and semi-structured interviews with raters supported these findings, further revealing a nonlinear relationship between cohesion and coherence, as well as the emergent influences of pronunciation and utterance fluency on coherence judgments. The study proposes an empirically grounded model of coherence in personal story generation speaking tasks, highlighting schematic structure and elaboration as key to listener perceptions of coherence. It empirically supports cognitive and functional discourse processing theories, offering pedagogical insights for enhancing L2 learners’ coherence and discourse competence.

t: Vocabulary knowledge and reading proficiency in extramural L2 English among ESCAPERS in Norway and Flanders
abs: This quantitative-dominant study discusses the relation between escapist reading and gaming, foreign/second language (L2) English vocabulary, and reading proficiency. Escapism, the act of temporarily escaping reality, is under-researched in L2 learning but relevant for inclusive learning environments and learner interests. The study addresses this gap by examining how 364 learners (aged 15–16) in Norway and Flanders performed on a vocabulary and reading test, respectively. Learners answered a questionnaire about informal/extramural English (EE), identifying 66 Readers, 70 Gamers, and 118 Reader + Gamers (doing both EE-activities). Across the sample, 170 Escapers and 27 so-called Profound escapers were identified. Descriptive and inferential analyses revealed that Readers and Gamers scored significantly higher than Non-readers and Non-gamers. Escapers significantly outperformed Non-escapers on both tests, and Profound escapers performed significantly better than all others. Differences between Norwegian and Flemish learners were non-significant. Regression analyses identified EE-reading as a predictor for vocabulary and reading proficiency, whereas EE-gaming predicted vocabulary only. The findings indicate that increased EE and escapism relate to higher L2 proficiency, which merits further research to better understand informal learning.

t: Change and Stability in Thesis and Dissertation Writing: The Evolution of an Academic Genre
Spatial policing: Race, surveillance, and the politics of community language schools in White public-school spaces
abs: This article draws on critically oriented scholarship at the intersection of surveillance, space, and race to explore the deep struggles over space between teachers and students at a public school in the U.S. and teachers and students at an Arabic community language school that rents the public-school facility on Saturdays. Evidence collected during two years of ethnographic fieldwork suggests that processes of racializing surveillance (Browne 2012; Selod 2018) were materially enacted by public school actors as spatial regimes that regulated the micro-level spatial practices of the community-school teachers and students. These regimes, which I call spatial policing, sanctioned how spaces (e.g. classrooms, whiteboards, desks) could or could not be used by the community-school teachers and students and regulated where they could sit and what they could use and say in the space. I argue that these regimes of spatial policing served to constitute the public school as a White public space (Hill 1998) and socialized the community-school teachers and students into invisible and apolitical subjectivities. The findings illuminate the ways by which the politics of space can offer a generative lens to understating how the marginalization of racialized language speakers is spatially enacted and how it affects the teaching and learning of language in education spaces.

t: Linguistic Approaches in English for Academic Purposes: Expanding the Discourse
