abs: Complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF) are essential indices of language development and performance (Vercellotti 2017). Numerous studies in applied linguistics and English for Academic Purposes (EAP) have explored these crucial factors and their relations to language use and academic success (e.g. Larsen-Freeman 2006; Biber et al. 2020). Nevertheless, relatively little scholarship has systematically investigated CAF in academic discourse through a linguistic lens. New approaches and perspectives are needed to broaden linguistic research in EAP and to bridge the gap between research insights and pedagogical practice. Linguistic Approaches in English for Academic Purposes: Expanding the Discourse represents a timely and valuable contribution. This edited volume, comprising an Introduction and three parts with a total of nine chapters, is curated by Milada Walková and contributed by a team of established scholars. The insights presented in this thought-provoking volume aim to help readers deepen their understanding of academic discourse, thereby enhancing their ability to express ideas clearly, appropriately, and persuasively within the contemporary global academic environment.

t: Expertise in Second Language Writing Instruction: Conceptual and Empirical Understandings
abs: Reforms in second language (L2) writing instructional approaches and technology-empowered education have brought transformative changes to L2 writing pedagogical landscapes. As L2 writing researchers and practitioners, we have observed that such changes can be ‘one man’s meat and another man’s poison’ for L2 writing teachers. Specifically, while many ‘novice’ and ‘experienced nonexpert’ teachers proactively adapt to changes and broaden their instructional repertoires, some expert teachers may, paradoxically, exhibit reduced confidence in adjusting their pedagogical practices. This phenomenon offers us a practical rationale for exploring L2 writing teacher expertise, an under-explored area in L2 writing research. Specifically, since the emergence of L2 writing as an independent field over the past four decades or so, scholarship has generated substantial insights into L2 writers and their writing development. By contrast, considerably less attention has been devoted to L2 writing teachers, let alone to systematic investigations into what constitutes expertise in L2 writing instruction, a ‘less travelled road’ characterized by Hirvela and Belcher (2022). It is in this context that Expertise in Second Language Writing Instruction: Conceptual and Empirical Understandings, edited by Hirvela and Belcher, capture our interest for its clear structure and accessible language. Building on and extending earlier calls to foreground L2 writing teacher expertise, it takes up the baton from previous disciplinary efforts to bring sustained attention to this under examined topic. By assembling a wide range of scholarly perspectives that employ diverse research approaches and analytical lenses, this edited volume is the first one to exclusively delve into L2 writing teacher expertise. Overall, we find it to be a timely and significant publication that not only addresses the long-standing ‘expertise gap’ but also provides valuable insights for both L2 writing teachers’ professional development and researchers’ empirical investigations.

t: Knowledge-making from a postgraduate writers’ circle: A Southern Reflectory
abs: This volume in Multilingual Matters’ Studies in Knowledge Production and Participation series builds on, and re-imagines, a rich tradition of work in writing studies and Academic Literacies which has emerged in the past three decades, in which scholars located outside the academy’s global ‘centre’ have played a leading role. The book is both a rich personal reflection on the author’s own practice as a writing circle facilitator, and a scholarly, deeply theorized post-qualitative enquiry into the nature of postgraduate writing as a knowledge-making practice. Written in lyrical style, it makes fewer concessions to the dry cadences of conventional academic prose than is usual in texts which constitute the body of scholarly published work which Thesen calls the ‘formal archive’, one of the guiding concepts of this book. Beneath the book’s playfulness and fluidity, however, lie a rigorous methodological and theoretical framing and a compelling auto/ethnographic data set (incorporating notes, sketches, gathered texts, interview-conversations and focus groups), persuading the reader that this is a serious, not merely impressionistic or quixotic, work. The reader is carried along via shifts and surprises as Thesen creates her ‘epistemic assemblage’ (p. 7), while always also making clear what she aims to do and why.

t: FOREIGN LANGUAGE LEARNING FROM AUDIOVISUAL INPUT: THE ROLE OF ORIGINAL VERSION TELEVISION BY PATTEMORE & GESA (SPRINGER, 2025)
abs: The proliferation of streaming platforms has significantly enhanced the accessibility of original version (OV) television, providing an unprecedented opportunity for second language (L2) learners to engage with authentic input. Yet, as Pattemore and Gesa emphasize in their timely edited volume, Foreign Language Learning from Audiovisual Input, the pedagogical potential of OV television across a wide range of linguistic features and languages remains underexplored. This collection, composed of six empirical studies and one narrative review, addresses this gap by offering a coherent roadmap for leveraging OV television to develop holistic, integrated, and creative L2 proficiency. The book opens with a succinct introduction by Pattemore and Gesa, who incisively identify three constraints in existing research: an over-reliance on English as the target language, a narrowed focus on the receptive knowledge of single words, and a comparative neglect of classroom application. The subsequent chapters systematically address these limitations, collectively creating a coherent narrative that frames OV television as a source of rich, multimodal input for second language development.
